author: reek
body: process-spawn-on-core hands the scheduler a child together with the core it must run on. From then on only that core's idle-dispatch, preempt scan or yield will claim it: every one of those paths skips a candidate whose affinity is neither -1 (any core) nor the id of the core doing the claiming.

author: reek
body: The child is pinned to core 2 and asked which core actually ran it. A core stamps its own id into the process it claims, so the child reads that stamp back out of its own table entry -- process-get-pid gives its slot, and the core id lives eight bytes into the entry. If affinity holds, the only core that could have claimed a child pinned to 2 is core 2, so the stamp reads 2.

author: reek
body: The test can fail, which is the point. If the pin were ignored and the boot processor claimed the child, the stamp would read 0 and the test would say AFFINITY VIOLATED. If a pinned child were never claimable at all, the wait would never return and the test would time out. Reporting the core the child actually ran on, rather than that it merely finished, is what distinguishes a respected pin from a child that happened to run somewhere.
